newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: FIVE FEARED DEAD AS CZECH FLOODING WORSENS.
newsitem.headline: FIVE FEARED DEAD AS CZECH FLOODING WORSENS.

text.p: Flooding due to heavy rain in the northeastern Czech Republic was blamed for five deaths on Monday, and officials issued calls for drinking water and emergency supplies as rivers to continue to rise.

Two women and three men were believed to have died as a result of the flooding which has swept away houses and has cut off dozens of people from rescue crews causing them to flee to their rooftops, the Czech news agency CTK reported.
The reports of the deaths have not been independently confirmed.
Numerous towns and villages lining tributaries to the Opava and Morava rivers have been inundated in several regions.
Hundreds of people, including children attending summer camps near the waters, have been evacuated, and rail and road transport has been suspended in some nearby areas.

Forecasts throughout much of the region expect more heavy rain to fall in the next 24 hours, threatening low lying areas including the country's third largest city Ostrava, and the industrial city of Zlin further downstream.
Officials fear the situation could spread into parts of eastern Bohemia, where tributaries on the upper parts of the Elbe and Upa rivers.
Roads, electricity, and telephone service has been disrupted in many parts of the northeast, and sources of clean drinking water have been made contaminated by the rising tide.
Disaster relief officials declared a state of emergency and the government has dispatched helicopters, soldiers, police and fire units from throughout the country to aid rescue operations.

"I would be very happy and would ask all who can offer help, to give whatever volume of drinking water, in whatever packaging, in tanks or in bottles," Ladislav Olejnicek, spokesman for the flood crisis team, told Czech radio.
Some hospitals lost their sources of drinking water, CTK said, and the waterworks in Ostrava had been cut off from several of its sources.
Early damage esitimates have already topped the two billion crowns as a result of flooding in the same region last year.
